title: Are the rules of grammar inherited or learned?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Linguists have long disputed whether the specific rules or grammar which govern each and every language are transmitted through culture, as part of the brain's general learning ability, or are internally generated with the help of genetically specified neural circuits that prescribe them. Since children learn to speak from those around them, there is no obvious way of determining exactly what is genetically inherited and what is learned, except by observing a new language being developed from the very start, something that happens very rarely.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A special opportunity to observe a new language and identify its genetically inherited elements has recently arisen. It is a sign language that is used in an isolated village inhabited by Bedouin people in the Negev desert, near the border with Jordan. Sign languages, commonly used by deaf people, possess all the properties of spoken language, including grammar, and differ only in the channel through which meaning is conveyed. Linguists hope to learn more about the brain's language machinery by identifying the features that the Bedouin sign language uses.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This language, known as Al Sayyid Bedouin Sign Language, is used by 3,500 inhabitants of a Bedouin village. The single founder of the village arrived 200 years ago from Egypt, and married a local woman. Two of the couple's five sons were deaf, as are about 150 members of the community today. The village has long been known to geneticists, but only recently have linguists begun to study its sign language. According to Dr Wendy Sandler, a researcher at the University of Haifa, the Bedouin sign language arose spontaneously and without outside influence. Dr Sandler adds that Bedouin sign language is not related to any sign languages in use nearby, and its word order differs from that of the spoken languages of the region.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Two aspects of the Bedouin sign language that look as if they come from an inherited grammatical machinery are a distinction between subject and object, and the preference for a specific word order in sentences, according to Dr Mark Aronoff of Stony Brook University in the USA. The word order in Bedouin sign language is subject-object-verb, the most common order amongst the world's languages. Dr Aronoff said that the emergence of a preferred order was the critical element, and that it was too early to tell if subject-object-verb is the particular order favored by the brain's neural circuitry.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Ann Senghas, of Barnard College in New York, has studied another emerging sign language in Nicaragua in Central America. She believes that the subject-object distinction and word order could be genetically inherited elements of all languages, but says that the preferred word order in Nicaraguan sign language keeps changing with each succeeding generation of children. The language has now acquired the signed equivalents of case endings—the variations used in languages like Latin to show if a word is the subject or object of a sentence. Word order can be less rigorous in languages that use case endings. The Bedouin sign language, which has no case endings, is still developing. The third generation of village children are signing twice as fast as their parents and grandparents and are using longer sentences, said Dr Carol Padden of the University of California, San Diego, USA. Dr Steven Pinker, a cognitive scientist at Harvard, said the Bedouin sign language, together with the work on Nicaraguan sign language and other studies, indicates that the human mind has the means to create all the grammatical structures necessary for full communication without the need for many generations of fine tuning, trial and error, and accumulation of traditions. The absence of case endings in the Bedouin sign language, however, was not surprising, Dr Pinker added, because these grammatical refinements are not necessary for communicating meaning, and often take many generations to develop.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have speculated that language evolved first in the form of a system of gestures, with sound taking over only later as the preferred channel of communication. Evidence that gesture is still deeply embedded in language can be seen in the fact that people gesticulate even when on the phone. Does the vigor and spontaneity of the Bedouin sign language, as well as the Nicaraguan example, support the idea that a gesture-based language evolved first? Dr Senghas said the two languages 'are not evidence about what came first', but confirm that gesture is an integral part of language.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The Bedouin sign language is unusual in being understood by the whole community, since hearing people use it to communicate with their deaf relatives. The signs have already become symbolic; the sign for man is the twirl of a finger to indicate a moustache, although men in the Bedouin village do not commonly have them now. The Bedouin village is not geographically remote—it is near a large fast food outlet—but has been socially isolated from other Bedouin people who have historically not mixed with the village inhabitants. The effects of modernization, however, are growing. Like most other children around the world, the deaf Bedouin children use the internet and are exposed to everything that it brings. Some observers question whether this Bedouin group will be able to withstand modernization and the ever-increasing number of marriages of its members with partners outside the community.
